cues.text: Welcome to Organic Halogens.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Classify the carbon bearing halogen before comparing reactions.
In a haloalkane, halogen is bonded to a saturated carbon.
In chlorobenzene, chlorine is directly attached to an aromatic ring carbon.
In benzyl chloride, chlorine is attached to a carbon outside the ring, so the
reacting environment is different.
Primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides are classified by how many
carbons are attached to the carbon carrying halogen.
A carbon halogen bond is generally polarized toward halogen, leaving the
carbon
susceptible to suitable nucleophiles.
Bond strength, leaving group stability, steric access and solvent all affect
reactivity.
For comparable simple substrates in many substitution settings, iodide is a
better leaving group than bromide, which is better than chloride; fluoride is
generally poor.
This ranking cannot replace a stated mechanism or conditions.
Also distinguish allylic and benzylic centres from vinylic and aryl centres.
A nearby pi system can stabilize an intermediate, but direct attachment to an
unsaturated carbon creates a different substitution problem.
Several routes produce organic halides, and they do not all use the same
mechanism.
Suitable hydrogen halides or reagents such as thionyl chloride can replace an
alcohol's hydroxyl group under appropriate conditions.
Adding hydrogen halide to an alkene instead consumes a pi bond and adds
hydrogen and halogen.
Radical halogenation of an alkane uses initiating conditions and can give
mixtures.
Aromatic ring halogenation commonly uses an electrophilic pathway with a
suitable Lewis acid.
In toluene, chlorine with iron three chloride under ring substitution
conditions can introduce chlorine on the ring, with ortho and para
preferences.
Under radical conditions such as light, substitution can instead occur at the
side chain.
Do not infer the reaction site from the molecular formula of the reagent
alone.
Preparation may also cause elimination, rearrangement or further substitution
depending on substrate and conditions.
Before writing an arrow, circle the carbon being changed and identify whether
the intended process replaces a group, adds across a multiple bond or changes
a
side chain.
Then verify the product's carbon skeleton.
In the S N two mechanism, a nucleophile approaches carbon from the side
opposite the leaving group.
Bond formation and departure occur in one concerted step.
A free carbocation is not an intermediate.
In the simple rate law, rate equals the rate constant times substrate
concentration times nucleophile concentration.
Doubling either concentration doubles the rate, and doubling both multiplies
it
by four, with temperature and other conditions unchanged.
Backside access becomes harder as the reaction centre is crowded.
Comparable methyl and primary alkyl substrates are therefore more accessible
than tertiary substrates for this pathway.
Polar aprotic solvents often support reactive anionic nucleophiles, although
the complete substrate and reagent combination must still be considered.
At a reacting stereogenic carbon, backside attack inverts the local geometry.
This does not automatically turn every R label into S, because priority
rankings may change in the product.
Reassign the configuration rather than treating a label as a physical
mechanism.
A stronger nucleophile cannot simply force an ordinary tertiary centre to
follow a favourable backside substitution path.
In a simple S N one mechanism, slow ionization first forms a carbocation
and leaving group.
Nucleophile capture occurs afterward.
The ideal rate law depends on substrate concentration alone, because
nucleophile participation is not part of the slow ionization step.
Doubling only nucleophile concentration therefore produces no direct rate
change in this ideal model.
A tertiary substrate can favour ionization under suitable conditions because
its carbocation is more stable than a simple primary one.
Benzylic and allylic intermediates may gain resonance stabilization.
Strongly ionizing media can assist separation of charged species.
A carbocation can rearrange when a more favourable structure is accessible, so
compare skeletons before declaring the final substitution product.
A planar carbocation permits attack from either face, allowing a stereogenic
substrate to lose optical purity.
Exact equal racemization is not guaranteed because ion pairing and nearby
groups can make the faces unequally accessible.
These are mechanistic tendencies, not a rule that every tertiary halide always
gives substitution: elimination can compete.
State the solvent, nucleophile and temperature before choosing a dominant
pathway.
In beta elimination, hydrogen is removed from a carbon adjacent to the carbon
carrying the leaving group.
A double bond forms between these alpha and beta carbons.
In the E two mechanism, base removes hydrogen as the leaving group departs in
the same step.
The simple rate depends on both substrate and base concentrations.
An appropriate anti periplanar arrangement helps the required orbital overlap;
ring conformations can therefore restrict which product forms.
Heating a suitable haloalkane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide commonly
favours elimination in elementary questions, while aqueous hydroxide often
favours substitution for suitable substrates.
These are contextual comparisons, not absolute switches.
Bromoethane with aqueous hydroxide can give ethanol; with hot alcoholic base
it
can give ethene.
A secondary butyl halide with a small base often gives but two ene as the
major
alkene, while bulky bases or geometric restrictions can change preferences.
First check that a beta hydrogen exists, then identify all possible adjacent
double bonds.
Distinguish the major product from the only possible product.
Ordinary chlorobenzene resists the usual alkyl substitution pathways.
The chlorine bearing carbon is sp two hybridized, and conjugation gives the
carbon chlorine bond partial double bond character.
Ordinary backside S N two displacement at that aromatic carbon is difficult.
A simple S N one route would require an unfavourable phenyl cation, so it is
not the usual alternative.
Benzyl chloride has its leaving group on a saturated carbon outside the ring
and must be considered separately.
Resistance does not mean all haloarenes are chemically inert.
Strong electron withdrawing groups, such as nitro groups in suitable ortho or
para positions relative to halogen, can activate a ring toward nucleophilic
aromatic substitution.
The intermediate and reaction pathway differ from ordinary alkyl substitution.
A meta nitro group does not provide the same direct resonance stabilization in
the usual addition elimination mechanism.
Harsh conditions can also allow other aromatic substitution pathways.
For an exam comparison, mark the exact attachment point, locate activating
substituents and read the conditions before ranking reactivity from a
memorized
halide list.
An appropriate organic halide can react with magnesium in dry ether to form a
Grignard reagent.
Its carbon has strongly basic and nucleophilic character.
Water or another sufficiently acidic proton can quench the reagent before a
planned carbon carbon bond forming reaction.
Ethylmagnesium bromide meeting water gives ethane as its organic product: the
ethyl carbon accepts a proton instead of adding to a later carbonyl reagent.
This is why dry conditions are chemically necessary.
When no acidic interference is present, reaction with an appropriate carbonyl
compound followed by work up can form a new carbon carbon bond, but the
precise
product depends on the carbonyl partner.
Wurtz coupling instead uses sodium with suitable alkyl halides in dry ether.
Two methyl halide units can couple to ethane.
Using different alkyl halides can give several homo and cross coupling
products, making the method poorly selective for one unsymmetrical alkane.
Count the carbons from both coupling partners and consider all pairings.
Do not confuse magnesium insertion with sodium coupling merely because both
start from an organic halide.
Some halogen compounds are studied for their properties and environmental
history as well as their reactions.
Chloroform has been used as a solvent and historically as an anaesthetic.
It has significant toxicity and can oxidize in air and light to phosgene.
Iodoform is associated with an older antiseptic use and with the yellow
product
formed in the iodoform test for suitable precursors.
Many chlorofluorocarbons persist long enough to reach the stratosphere, where
chlorine radicals can catalyse ozone destruction.
D D T has a history of insecticidal use and concerns involving persistence
and bioaccumulation.
These chemical facts should be connected with molecular stability and reaction
pathways rather than reduced to a list of names.
For a product question, record four things: substrate, reagent, solvent and
conditions.
Decide whether substitution, elimination, proton transfer or coupling is
plausible.
Check the carbon skeleton, charges and the presence of beta hydrogen where
required.
Apply a rate law only to the stated mechanism.
The practice questions review those choices; fuller stereochemical drawings
and
additional preparation routes remain for further lessons.
An S N two substitution occurs through a concerted bond making and bond
breaking event.
The incoming nucleophile approaches opposite the leaving group, producing
inversion of the spatial arrangement at a reacting stereogenic carbon.
This is often called Walden inversion.
It does not imply that every printed R descriptor must change to S, because
replacing a group can change the priority order used to assign the descriptor.
First follow the actual three dimensional arrangement, then assign priorities
to the product.
A methyl substrate has no stereogenic carbon, so its S N two reaction cannot
be
described as producing a pair of carbon enantiomers merely because backside
attack occurred.
The bimolecular rate law refers to the elementary substitution step and
depends
on both substrate and nucleophile concentration under that model.
Steric crowding near the reacting carbon can hinder the required approach.
A tertiary substrate therefore does not become a good ordinary S N two
substrate just because a strong nucleophile is present.
Separate reaction mechanism, spatial inversion and the final naming descriptor
rather than treating them as one memorized word.
An S N one model begins with ionization to a carbocation and a leaving group.
A simple trigonal planar carbocation can be approached from either face, so
substitution at a suitable stereogenic centre can give both configurations.
The result is often described as racemization, but real ion pairs and solvent
cages can make the proportions unequal.
Do not promise an exact fifty fifty mixture without the additional assumptions
needed for equal access.
Carbocation intermediates can also rearrange by suitable hydride or alkyl
shifts when a more favourable cation is accessible.
Such a shift moves a bonding pair together with the migrating group and
changes
which carbon bears the positive charge.
It is not a resonance contributor that leaves every hydrogen attachment
unchanged.
Product prediction therefore needs the substrate structure and conditions,
rather than the S N one label alone.
The rate determining ionization model gives first order dependence on
substrate
when that step controls the observed rate.
A favourable carbocation does not exclude competing elimination, especially
when the surrounding conditions encourage proton removal.
An alkyl halide may undergo substitution or elimination, and the reagent label
alone is not a complete prediction.
In a common introductory comparison, aqueous hydroxide can replace bromide in
bromoethane to give ethanol, while heated alcoholic base can promote
elimination to ethene.
Both products retain the two carbon skeleton, but they change different bonds.
Substitution makes a new carbon oxygen bond; elimination removes a beta
hydrogen and the leaving group to form a carbon carbon double bond.
A beta hydrogen must be available for this ordinary elimination.
With more substituted substrates, base strength and size, solvent, temperature
and geometry influence the competition and alkene distribution.
In an E two process, the relevant beta carbon hydrogen bond and carbon leaving
group bond favour an antiperiplanar arrangement.
A bulky base can alter which beta hydrogen is removed, so a single major
alkene
rule is not universal.
Methyl halides lack a beta carbon and cannot undergo the usual beta
elimination
to an alkene.
Inspect the actual substrate and competing paths before using a preparation
shortcut.
An ambidentate reagent can connect through different atoms, so product
connectivity matters.
In the usual introductory alkyl halide comparison, ionic cyanide such as
potassium cyanide favours carbon bonded nitrile formation, while silver
cyanide
is associated with isocyanide formation through nitrogen under the specified
preparation conditions.
Do not draw those products as interchangeable resonance forms.
For bromoethane reacting by nitrile formation, the two carbon ethyl group
acquires the cyanide carbon, producing propanenitrile with three carbons.
Subsequent nitrile hydrolysis can give propanoic acid after the appropriate
workup.
Carbon counting exposes a common error: the product is not ethanoic acid
merely
because the starting halide was ethyl.
An isocyanide has the alkyl group attached to nitrogen instead and requires
separate reaction reasoning.
These are reagent dependent preparation patterns, not a claim that every
substrate reacts equally well.
The normal nucleophilic substitution limitations still apply, particularly
steric hindrance for a direct S N two pathway.
Always identify the atom making the new bond before naming the product or
planning the next conversion.
A halogen attached directly to an aromatic ring is aryl, while one attached to
an alkene carbon is vinylic.
A benzyl halide instead has the halogen on a saturated carbon directly next to
the aromatic ring.
These positions are not equivalent.
Benzyl chloride contains a carbon chlorine bond at an S P three carbon,
whereas
chlorobenzene attaches chlorine to an aromatic S P two carbon.
Ordinary alkyl substitution shortcuts cannot simply be transferred to
chlorobenzene or a vinyl halide.
In an aryl carbon halogen bond, conjugation and the geometry of the carbon
framework affect reactivity.
Suitable activating substituents and forcing conditions can enable other
aromatic substitution pathways, but that does not establish a normal freely
formed phenyl carbocation mechanism.
Benzyl substrates can be reactive in substitution because their adjacent
aromatic system can stabilize relevant intermediates or transition states,
subject to the actual pathway and substituents.
Classify the reaction centre first, then inspect the nucleophile, solvent and
activation pattern.
The presence of a benzene ring somewhere in the molecule is not enough to
classify every carbon halogen bond as aryl.
A named reaction is a useful map only when the substrate and conditions match.
In the standard Finkelstein comparison, an appropriate alkyl chloride or
bromide undergoes halogen exchange with iodide in acetone.
The sodium chloride or bromide formed has low solubility in this medium, so
its
precipitation helps drive the exchange.
For a suitable primary substrate, the substitution can follow a concerted
backside attack.
The carbon skeleton stays unchanged: a two carbon alkyl bromide gives a two
carbon alkyl iodide, rather than adding the iodide as a new carbon fragment.
The Swarts name instead refers to preparing alkyl fluorides by halogen
exchange
using suitable metal fluorides.
These labels do not make every aryl or vinyl halide behave like a primary
alkyl
substrate.
Chlorobenzene, for example, does not enter ordinary backside substitution at
its ring carbon simply because iodide is present.
Nor should a solvent precipitation argument be transferred to water without
checking salt solubilities.
Use the reaction names to identify the exchanged atom, the preserved carbon
framework and the stated substrate class.
Product bookkeeping is different from an experimental preparation protocol.
Carbon coupling needs a selectivity check as well as a carbon count.
In the elementary Wurtz scheme, two alkyl halide fragments couple in the
presence of sodium, with salt as another product.
If only one suitable alkyl halide is used, joining two identical fragments
gives a symmetrical alkane.
Mixing methyl and ethyl halides does not guarantee pure propane.
The possible simple coupling connectivities are methyl with methyl, methyl
with
ethyl, and ethyl with ethyl, giving ethane, propane and butane respectively.
The two possible orders of joining methyl to ethyl describe the same propane
connectivity, not two different constitutional products.
Thus the elementary list contains three alkane connectivities, not four.
This count is not a prediction of equal amounts or a fixed statistical yield.
Different substrate reactivities, side reactions and conditions affect the
actual product mixture.
Wurtz coupling is generally more useful for an appropriate symmetrical target
than as an unqualified route to one unsymmetrical alkane from a mixed feed.
Balance two sodium atoms for two halide ions in the simple overall coupling
equation, and keep product identity separate from an assumed product
distribution.
An organomagnesium reagent contributes its carbon fragment to a carbonyl
compound in the familiar Grignard addition model.
Take methylmagnesium bromide and acetaldehyde, followed by a separate
protonation step.
The carbon bearing magnesium forms a bond to the former carbonyl carbon.
Acetaldehyde supplies two carbon atoms and the methyl fragment supplies one,
giving a three carbon alcohol, propan two ol.
The carbonyl oxygen becomes an alkoxide oxygen first and is protonated later;
the alcohol proton need not come from the original aldehyde.
Compare a methyl reagent with formaldehyde: one plus one carbon gives ethanol,
a primary alcohol.
With propanone, three plus one gives a four carbon tertiary alcohol.
These examples classify the alcohol by the groups on its oxygen bearing
carbon,
not by the total carbon count alone.
Water or another suitable proton donor present before addition can instead
consume the organomagnesium reagent through an acid base reaction, producing
the corresponding hydrocarbon.
Therefore carbonyl addition and proton quenching are competing descriptions
only after the order of exposure is specified.
This is a connectivity and stoichiometry exercise, not a laboratory handling
recipe.
A product count must state whether it counts connectivity or stereochemistry.
Consider two bromobutane as a substrate and compare idealized substitution
with
elimination.
Replacing bromine by hydroxyl at the same carbon gives butan two ol as the
substitution connectivity.
In elimination, removing a beta hydrogen from either adjacent carbon can place
the double bond at the end of the chain or in its middle.
The constitutional alkene products are but one ene and but two ene.
The internal alkene has two distinct groups at each double bond carbon, so it
can occur as E and Z geometrical isomers.
The terminal alkene has a carbon bearing two hydrogens and therefore has no E
Z
pair.
Counting alkene stereoisomers separately gives three alkene products in this
elementary set, while counting alkene connectivities gives two.
This enumeration does not claim that all are formed in equal amounts or that
substitution is absent under every elimination condition.
Base size, solvent, temperature and the available conformations affect
competition and selectivity.
In an E two pathway, the removed hydrogen and leaving group require a suitable
antiperiplanar arrangement; a flat formula alone does not determine the
relative yields.
An alcohol does not usually undergo a simple substitution by expelling free
hydroxide without activation.
For suitable primary and secondary alcohols, phosphorus tribromide can enable
conversion of the carbon oxygen bond into a carbon bromine bond.
The net bookkeeping equation uses three alcohol molecules for one phosphorus
tribromide, forming three alkyl bromides and phosphorous acid.
This balances oxygen and hydrogen as well as bromine.
For a stipulated quantitative conversion of zero point zero three zero zero
mole ethanol, the theoretical phosphorus tribromide amount from this equation
is zero point zero one zero zero mole and bromoethane amount zero point zero
three zero zero mole.
This is stoichiometric bookkeeping, not a complete experimental reagent
prescription.
A suitable secondary stereogenic alcohol can undergo inversion at the reacting
carbon in the usual substitution pathway.
That does not imply an automatic reversal of its R or S letter without
checking
product priorities.
Tertiary substrates do not follow this same simple backside displacement
model.
Choose the actual substrate class and leaving group activation before copying
a
reagent rule onto every alcohol.
A vicinal dihalide contains halogens on adjacent carbon atoms.
In an appropriate double dehydrohalogenation sequence, two eliminations can
convert that skeleton into an alkyne.
For one two dibromoethane, the starting formula is two carbons, four hydrogens
and two bromines.
Removing two hydrogen bromide units leaves two carbons and two hydrogens, the
formula of ethyne.
The first elimination produces a vinyl halide with a carbon carbon double
bond.
The second elimination acts on that different bonding environment and
generally
requires a suitably strong base; it is not simply a repeat of the easiest
alkyl
halide reaction.
The overall carbon count remains two.
Formal loss of two hydrogen bromide units counts the two elimination events,
but does not establish that exactly two equivalents of base suffice in every
preparative system.
A terminal alkyne can also undergo deprotonation by a sufficiently strong
base,
followed by separate protonation on workup.
Distinguish transformation stoichiometry, intermediate identity and reagent
consumption rather than treating a net atom ledger as a complete mechanism or
procedure.
The fate of a Grignard reagent depends on whether it meets a carbon
electrophile or a proton source.
Ethylmagnesium bromide contains a two carbon organic group.
Addition to carbon dioxide followed by separate protonation gives propanoic
acid, whose carboxyl carbon came from carbon dioxide.
The product has three carbons.
Direct proton quenching of the same reagent instead gives ethane, retaining
only the original two carbons.
Phenylmagnesium bromide similarly gives benzoic acid after carbon dioxide
addition and protonation, so six ring carbons become a seven carbon acid.
These transformations do not imply that a carboxylic acid itself is an
interchangeable carbon dioxide reagent: an acidic proton can consume the
organomagnesium reagent by acid base reaction.
The initial addition product in carboxylation is a metal carboxylate, not the
fully protonated acid.
Other acidic groups or reactive functions in the substrate can prevent a
simple
Grignard route.
Track the source of the added carbon and the timing of protonation before
choosing between a carbon forming reaction and a reagent destroying quench.
A substituent can influence overall reaction speed and positional preference
in
different ways.
In ordinary electrophilic aromatic substitution, chlorine withdraws electron
density inductively, making chlorobenzene less reactive than benzene under
comparable conditions.
Yet its lone pairs can contribute resonance stabilization to the intermediates
for ortho and para attack relative to meta attack.
Thus a halogen is a deactivating ortho and para director, not an activating
group merely because of those preferred positions.
For a simple nitration comparison, ortho and para chloronitrobenzene are the
usual favoured positional products, while the carbon chlorine bond remains
intact.
This is not nucleophilic aromatic substitution, where a nucleophile replaces
the leaving group under an appropriate activation pattern.
Nor does an ortho para label specify a universal numerical product ratio.
Steric effects, electrophile identity and reaction conditions affect the
distribution.
Keep three separate questions visible: what kind of substitution occurs, which
bond changes, and how the existing substituent affects rate and position.
A single directing arrow cannot answer all three.
Chair geometry can restrict elimination before alkene substitution preferences
are compared.
In the ordinary cyclohexane chair E two model, a leaving group and the removed
beta hydrogen must be trans diaxial: axial on adjacent carbons and pointing in
opposite directions.
Consider a supplied chair with bromine axial up at carbon one.
Carbon two has methyl axial down, so its hydrogen is equatorial and cannot
supply the required axial hydrogen on that side.
Carbon six instead has an axial down hydrogen.
Elimination can therefore form the bond between carbons one and six in this
chair, rather than the more substituted alternative between one and two.
The methyl group occupies a needed hydrogen position; it does not itself
become
a leaving group.
If bromine is equatorial in another chair, the ordinary trans diaxial pathway
requires a suitable ring flip first.
A flip exchanges axial and equatorial positions while retaining each
substituent's up or down identity.
This is an analysis of the supplied chair geometry, not a universal rule that
the most substituted alkene always wins or that all equatorial halides are
permanently unable to eliminate.
A nucleophile ranking must state the solvent and the reaction being compared.
Polar protic solvents such as water or alcohols can form hydrogen bond shells
around anionic nucleophiles.
This stabilization can reduce their availability for backside attack on a
suitable alkyl substrate.
Polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or dimethyl sulfoxide often support
faster S N two reactions of suitable dissolved anionic nucleophiles, because
the solvation environment is different.
Do not call those anions completely unsolvated or infer an identical rate
increase for every salt.
Counterions, solubility, substrate crowding, temperature and competing
elimination still matter.
In an original matched rate dataset, let the same substrate and nucleophile
concentrations give rate constant zero point zero one zero and zero point two
zero zero litre per mole per second in two stated solvents.
The second reaction is twenty times faster at the same concentrations, but
this
ratio is supplied evidence for that comparison rather than a universal solvent
constant.
Basicity concerns proton acceptance, while nucleophilicity concerns reaction
with the electrophilic substrate; the two descriptors need not give one
solvent
independent ordering.
A silver halide precipitate reports available halide ions, not merely a
halogen
atom somewhere in an organic formula.
In a supplied silver nitrate in ethanol comparison, ionization prone tertiary,
benzylic or allylic halides may release halide more readily than an ordinary
primary substrate.
Silver ion can itself assist halide departure, so this is not a measurement of
an entirely unaffected isolated carbon halogen bond.
Aryl and vinyl halides do not follow the same ordinary ionization pathway.
A negative or slow result therefore does not prove that an unknown contains no
covalently bonded halogen.
Time to visible precipitation also depends on temperature, solvent
composition,
concentrations, mixing and the detection threshold.
Compare known reference compounds under matching conditions before assigning a
structural class.
The precipitate colour or its subsequent solubility may help distinguish the
halide, but one timing observation alone does not uniquely identify an organic
molecule or prove a single mechanism under all conditions.
This chapter interprets a stipulated test system rather than giving an
experimental recipe or transferring its ranking to a polar aprotic S N two
reaction.
Elemental analysis and direct substitution tests answer different questions.
In the standard sodium fusion concept, covalently bound halogen is converted
into an ionic form so a prepared extract can be examined for chloride, bromide
or iodide.
Simply mixing an unchanged organochlorine compound with aqueous silver nitrate
need not release its chlorine as chloride.
The analysis scheme also needs controls on the reagents and interfering ions.
Introducing hydrochloric acid would add chloride from outside the sample and
could give silver chloride even when the sample contributed none.
The prescribed nitric acid medium avoids that particular added chloride
source.
Cyanide or sulfide in an untreated extract can also interfere with silver
precipitation, which is why the specified interference removal is part of the
analytical scheme.
This is interpretation of a prepared extract and its controls, not
instructions
for conducting sodium fusion or acid treatment.
Once ionic chloride is independently established, the net precipitation
equation is one silver ion plus one chloride giving one silver chloride
formula
unit.
Keep the original organic molecule, the converted extract species and reagent
contamination as three separate sources of evidence.
